inlines.text: 引言

blocks.text: 过去几年中，Meta 的 TorchTitan 已成为 PyTorch 生态中大规模生成式 AI 模型训练的首选净室参考平台。TorchTitan 完全基于 PyTorch 原生扩展原语构建，为 Llama 3、Qwen 3 和 FLUX 等旗舰级稠密模型与混合专家（MoE）架构的预训练提供了一个无拘束、高度模块化的展示平台。

blocks.text: 为什么选择 TPU 上的 TorchTitan

inlines.text: 为什么选择 TPU 上的 TorchTitan

blocks.text: Google 和 Meta 没有要求工程团队自行发明定制的 TPU 分片策略，或从零手写底层 XLA 通信 pass，而是直接在 TorchTitan 内部共同开发了 TPU 原生执行 pass。TorchTitan 是在 Google Cloud TPU 上扩展 PyTorch 的权威载体。

blocks.text: 模型定义与模型分区解耦

inlines.text: 模型定义与模型分区解耦

blocks.text: TorchTitan 中的模型定义使用纯单设备 PyTorch（nn.Module）编写，不含 CUDA 专用代码。集合通信要么由可组合的框架层（如 FSDP）插入，要么由声明式分片计划（如张量并行）插入，要么作为后端专用插件（如 MoE 层）插入。TorchTPU 支持 C10D 集合通信 API 和 PyTorch DeviceMesh 抽象。二者结合，使 TPU 路径能够为模型选择应用哪些并行方式，以及使用哪些实现。

inlines.text: 可插拔架构

blocks.text: TorchTitan 从配置树构建模型，并且该配置树可以在模型构建之前被重写。这提供了一种简洁的方式，将模型的各个块替换为在 TPU 上运行更好的版本，而无需改动模型定义或共享的训练器循环。

blocks.text: 我们正在积极使用这一方案。TPU recipe 用 Splash Attention 替代标准注意力——这是一种 Pallas 内核，能够处理因果、滑动窗口和打包文档掩码，而无需将注意力矩阵实际物化；用融合 Pallas 内核替代最终投影和交叉熵损失，该内核从不将完整的 logits 张量写入 HBM；并用分组 Pallas 内核替代 MoE 专家矩阵乘法。每个内核都是通过 TorchTPU 的 torch.tpu.pallas.jax_op 装饰器将 JAX 函数转换为 PyTorch 自定义算子，这就是新内核所需的全部粘合代码。每个替换都是一个配置开关，因此 recipe 可以将其开启，测试也可以将其与被替换的普通 PyTorch 路径进行对比。内核可以来自 tokamax，这是面向 TPU 和 GPU 的 OpenXLA 内核库。

blocks.text: 编译友好的 FSDP 实现

inlines.text: 编译友好的 FSDP 实现

blocks.text: FSDP2 是围绕 GPU 执行模型构建的。它的 all-gather 和 reduce-scatter 从模块钩子中作为显式集合通信调用发出，与计算的重叠来自于在专用 CUDA 流上运行它们并与事件同步。这些对编译器来说都是不可见的：集合通信位于被追踪区域之外，因此在 TPU 上，torch.compile 区域会在每个 FSDP 钩子处中断，整步图根本无法被捕获。TorchTPU 仅提供空操作的流和事件对象，以便 FSDP2 能够运行；XLA 并不需要它们，因为它根据数据依赖来调度工作。

blocks.text: SimpleFSDP 则采取了编译器的视角。参数分片是一种 DTensor 参数化：读取模块的权重会执行从分片到复制的 redistribute，这就是 all-gather，而其自动求导的反向传播就是 reduce-scatter。没有钩子，也没有显式的集合通信调用，因此这两个集合通信都是被追踪图中的普通节点，无论该图是逐块的 torch.compile 区域，还是 Graph Trainer 的单次 make_fx 步骤。XLA 编译器会在需要它们的矩阵乘法之前调度 all-gather，并在单个程序内将 reduce-scatter 与反向计算重叠。混合精度是同一机制的一部分，即在该 redistribute 上设置 gather dtype（bf16 参数）和 reduce dtype（fp32 或 bf16 梯度）的策略。多切片场景下的混合分片是在二维网格上的相同代码：在切片内通过 ICI 进行分片，在切片间通过 DCN 进行复制。

blocks.text: 1. 建立基线

inlines.text: 1. 建立基线
选择步骤的执行方式：eager、compile 或 Graph Trainer。
Eager 模式几乎无需更改即可在 TPU 上运行 PyTorch 模型，这使其成为引入模型和调试模型的正确场所。它不是性能配置：每个操作都是自己的程序，TPU 在启动之间空闲。TorchTPU 的
延迟融合 eager 模式
（--tpu_config.eager_mode=DEFER_AND_FUSE）通过让 XLA 跨操作边界融合，在无需更改代码的情况下恢复部分性能，并且 recipes 保持其开启以覆盖编译区域之外的任何内容。启用
逐块 torch.compile
（--compile.enable）是将调试配置转变为性能配置的关键：每个 transformer 块成为单个 XLA 程序，因此其操作被融合，一次启动而不是逐个启动，并与块的集合通信一起调度。块必须可追踪，这排除了其中依赖数据的 Python，这就是模型所放弃的全部。
Graph Trainer 更进一步
（--tpu_config.use_graph_trainer），让整个训练步骤——前向、损失、反向和优化器更新——被捕获为一个程序。整个步骤必须可追踪，你得到的是一个完全没有 eager 胶水的步骤，加上第 5 步中的大模型技术。
使用 SimpleFSDP 和混合精度策略进行分片。
SimpleFSDP 将分片表达为

追踪图中的集合通信操作（--parallelism.use_simple_fsdp），因此编译器可以针对其周围的矩阵乘法来调度 all-gather 和 reduce-scatter。FSDP2 本身针对 eager 性能进行了优化，但这也使其难以追踪进图。将其与 bf16 参数和 fp32 梯度归约搭配使用：计算以 bf16 运行，而主权重和归约保持 fp32，这是每个 TPU 配方都采用的设置。
对于大模型（约 100B+ 参数），启用 scan 或拆分图，并卸载激活值。
随着深度增加，单个展开的步骤图会停止编译，并且它会保持每一层保存的输入存活直到反向传播。
对层进行 Scan
（--tpu_config.use_scan_layers）将解码器作为单个循环体运行，因此编译时间和内存不再随深度增长，并将这一个堆叠的激活值卸载到主机内存；这是 Qwen3 235B 和 Llama 3 405B 采用的路径。
图拆分器
（--tpu_config.use_graph_split）保持层展开，但将前向和反向，以及可选的每个层组，编译为单独的程序，并在其间卸载激活值。两者都构建在 Graph Trainer 之上。

inlines.text: 2. 调优计算与内核
开启 Pallas 内核。
Splash attention
（--splash_attention_kernel.use_splash_attention_kernel）从不物化注意力矩阵，并处理因果、滑动窗口和打包文档掩码；它在长序列长度下最为重要。
融合线性交叉熵损失

（配方中的 PallasCrossEntropyLoss）一次一个词表分块地计算 LM-head 矩阵乘法、softmax 和损失，因此完整的 logits 张量永远不会写入 HBM。它的主要价值在于内存，下一步将其转化为吞吐量。对于 MoE 模型，分组专家矩阵乘法和成对的 gate/up 内核（use_pallas_paired_grouped_mm）用每层一个内核取代了对专家的循环。这些都是配方中的开关，并且每个都与其替代的普通 PyTorch 路径进行了测试对比。
调优内核分块大小。
Splash attention、融合损失和 MoE 内核各自暴露其块大小（sa_block_* 等），默认值只是起点而非最优值。根据模型形状和 TPU 代际，在限定的 VMEM 预算（xla_tpu_scoped_vmem_limit_kib）内调优它们，并预期在 Trillium 上调优的值不会延续到 Ironwood。配方中包含了每个模型和拓扑的调优值。

blocks.text: 3. 优化内存与批大小

inlines.text: 3. 优化内存与批大小
提高批大小。
在小规模下，每芯片批大小是最大的单一杠杆，因为它提高了每个启动程序所做的工作量。将其推高直到模型受限于 HBM；融合损失和注意力内核正是释放内存以实现这一点的关键。在大切片上，请记住全局批大小是每芯片批大小乘以芯片数量，因此应将其设置为模型能够使用的规模，而不是芯片能够容纳的规模

XLA 和 libtpu 标志

inlines.text: FLUX.1

blocks.text: FLUX.1 是一个 120 亿参数的扩散 Transformer，这使它成为检验上述方法并非只适用于 LLM 的有用案例。我们在 TPU v6e-8 上以 1024x1024 分辨率训练它，使用 bf16 的 FSDP 和三个样本的批大小。开箱即用，在启用 FSDP2 和完整激活检查点的 eager 模式下，一步耗时 11.49 秒。按顺序应用该方法后，耗时逐阶段下降。延迟且融合的 eager 执行将 HLO 模块调用次数减少了 28%，步骤耗时降至 9.95 秒（提升 15.5%）。用 SimpleFSDP 替换 FSDP2 后，步骤耗时降至 6.52 秒（提升 52.6%）：跟踪显示主要耗时在 FSDP2 于每次 all-gather 前将参数分片复制到扁平暂存缓冲区，之后再复制回各参数张量；SimpleFSDP 直接对每个参数执行 all-gather，因此暂存缓冲区和两次复制都消失了（参见上文 SimpleFSDP 部分）。splash attention 内核配合序列打包和 segment id，使没有 MXU 周期浪费在填充上，将步骤耗时降至 5.55 秒（提升 17.5%），而逐块 torch.compile 将大型子图而非细粒度模块交给 XLA，并将控制流移出 Python 解释器，将耗时降至 3.02 秒（提升 83.8%）。

blocks.text: MuseGlimmer

inlines.text: MuseGlimmer

blocks.text: Muse Glimmer 30B 是一个现代稠密解码器：52 层，分组查询注意力，32 个查询头和 2 个键值头，202k token 词表并带有软上限输出头，层模式混合了滑动窗口注意力和全局注意力，每第四层跳过 RoPE。这个案例展示了有多少工作可以开箱即用。模型定义、并行化和训练循环在 TPU 上无需改动即可运行；移植工作归结为两个模型特定的部分。上游使用 FlexAttention 实现滑动窗口模式，而它没有 TPU 后端，因此第一步是实现一个窗口化 SDPA 内层注意力，精确复现窗口并提供正确性基线，在 CPU 上与上游进行核对。第二部分是融合交叉熵内核，我们对其进行了扩展，在计算损失时对每个词表分块应用软上限，因此 202k 宽的 logits 永远不需要被物化；否则仅 LM 头就会主导内存占用。其他所有内容，包括Graph Trainer 封装，都是标准的接入流程，每个功能都在标志位之后并配有各自的测试。最终得到的配方在 64 个 v7x 芯片（一个 4x4x4 切片）上训练 30B 模型，序列长度为 16,384，每个设备一个序列，使用 Graph Trainer 加 SimpleFSDP 和 fp32 梯度归约，达到每芯片每秒 5,848 个 token，MFU 约为 44%。

blocks.text: Qwen3 235B

inlines.text: Qwen3 235B

blocks.text: Qwen3-235B-A22B 是这一组中最大的 MOE 模型：94 层，128 个专家，每个 token 激活 8 个，2350 亿参数，其中每个 token 激活 220 亿。它正是用来检验 playbook 中大模型那一半的案例。在这个深度上，把整个展开的 step 编译成一个程序并不可行：XLA 在编译时为程序的每个缓冲区做规划，而一个平铺展开的 94 层图在一步能运行之前所需的 HBM 就超过了芯片容量，同时其编译时间随每一层增长。要让它跑起来，意味着必须启用大模型两条 Graph Trainer 路径之一。Scan over layers 是 XLA 原生的方案，也是 JAX 和 MaxText 所依赖的同一构造：94 个相同的层变成一个编译后的循环体，于是编译时间和程序大小不再随深度增长。graph splitter 则是更灵活的替代方案：它保持层展开，但把捕获的 step 切分成逐层的可执行文件，这对任何类型的层都有效（且不要求各层相同）。我们为该模型同时运行了两种方案，结果相差在几个百分点以内。无论哪种方式，在序列长度 4096、每设备 16 条序列时，激活值都放不进 HBM，因此两条路径都会把层激活值卸载到主机内存，并在反向传播时预取回来。

blocks.text: 我们还使用该模型测试了 TorchTPU 的扩展能力，从 64 个芯片一直到 8,192 芯片的 v7x pod 规模，涵盖单切片和多切片两种配置。TPU 切片是一组通过 芯片间互连（ICI）直接相连的芯片；多切片让单个训练任务跨越多个通过数据中心网络（DCN）连接的切片，从而让任务规模突破单个最大切片的限制。在切片内部，我们通过 ICI 运行 FSDP，将参数、梯度和优化器状态分片到该切片的各个芯片上；跨切片时，模型被复制，梯度每步通过 DCN 进行一次 all-reduce，因此较慢网络上的唯一流量就是一次梯度归约，且与反向传播重叠。这就是混合分片数据并行（HSDP），也是 2,048 至 8,192 芯片运行所采用的方案，以 1,024 芯片切片作为分片组。整个过程中框架表现符合预期：从 64 芯片扩展到 8,192 芯片，每芯片吞吐量仅下降 8%（从每芯片每秒 4,568 个 token 降至 4,208 个 token），在芯片数量增加 128 倍的情况下接近线性扩展。需要说明一点：对于这一规模的模型，超过约 1K 芯片的数据并行属于扩展性实验，而非训练配方。这是一次弱扩展运行：每设备批大小在增加芯片时保持不变，因此全局批大小随芯片数量增长，在 8k 芯片时大于训练该模型实际会使用的批大小。该运行所展示的是框架、编译器和集合通信在该规模下依然可靠，而非这是应当采用的训练配置。

blocks.text: TorchTitan TPU 的 HuggingFace Transformers 建模后端

inlines.text: TorchTitan TPU 的 HuggingFace Transformers 建模后端

blocks.text: 上述三个案例研究都是深度剖析：一次只针对一个模型，每次改动背后都有对齐测试和性能分析。而一个刚接触 TPU 的团队通常面临不同的问题。他们已有一个正在训练的模型，往往是 Hugging Face 上的模型，而且很可能并不是 TorchTitan 为 TPU 提供的模型。他们最终可能确实想榨干每一分性能，但首先需要一种简单的方法让它先跑起来。这正是 Transformers 建模后端所解决的问题：它根据 Hub id 从 Transformers 库构建模型，并通过 TorchTitan 的训练器和并行策略（而非模型自带的）来运行。在 TPU 上，该后端有一条 TorchTPU 通道，采用单一配置，对任何受支持的检查点应用优化手册中的前几级优化，且无需修改模型代码：用 SimpleFSDP 替代 FSDP2、按块 torch.compile、将 splash attention 内核注册为注意力实现并接入 transformers 注意力接口，使模型自身的注意力调用落到该内核上、将融合 Pallas 交叉熵直接接收最终隐藏状态和输出头权重而非物化 logits，以及对于混合专家检查点，用 TPU 分组矩阵乘专家替代可移植实现。该后端支持的大多数稠密架构都能以这种方式未经修改地训练；混合专家检查点走同一路径，但尚不支持专家并行。这些都无法达到上文手工调优的数字，但对于尚无 TPU 配方的模型而言，这是一个可运行且效率尚可的首次运行方案，也是判断该模型是否值得投入定制配方的途径。

blocks.text: 路线图

inlines.text: 路线图

blocks.text: 路线图沿五条线展开：生产就绪、精度、硬件、并行和模型。在生产就绪方面，配方获得了在 Google Cloud 上长时间运行所期望的运维工具：与 ML Goodput Measurement 库集成，使一次运行能够报告其芯片时间中有多少转化为保留的训练进度，以及其余部分去了哪里；以及与 GKE 上的 Multi-Tier Checkpointing 集成，它将检查点保存在本地内存和集群内副本中，并以 Cloud Storage 作为持久层，使大型作业能够频繁保存并快速恢复。在精度方面，目前为 Llama 3 70B 提供的 float8 配方基于 torchao 的 Float8Linear 和 v7x 的原生 fp8 矩阵乘法构建，将扩展到其余模型集。在硬件方面，Google 已宣布其第八代 TPU，即用于预训练的 TPU 8t 和用于推理与强化学习的 TPU 8i，TorchTitan 将在它们于 Google Cloud 上可用时予以支持，并沿用相同的配方。在并行方面，MoE 内核的专家并行是前面提到的未完成项，长上下文训练紧随其后，因为百万 token 上下文窗口如今已是前沿模型的常态。在模型方面，目标是从 Qwen3-235B 往上的下一个规模：Qwen3.8-Max，一个 2.4 万亿参数的专家混合模型，以及 Kimi K3，2.8 万亿参数，在大多数层上用 Kimi Delta Attention 替代标准注意力，这将同时考验内核插件路径和扩展路径。

blocks.text: 总结

inlines.text: 总结

blocks.text: TPU 上的 TorchTitan 不再是一个实验。相同的代码库和纯 PyTorch 模型定义在最多 1,024 个芯片上以约 57% MFU 训练 Llama 3 405B，并在单个切片中最多 1,024 个芯片上运行 Qwen3 235B——一个专家混合模型。在固定每芯片批次的弱扩展测试中，Qwen3 235B 从 64 到 8,192 个芯片保持了 92% 的每芯片吞吐量。这表明框架、编译器和集合通信在 pod 规模下依然稳固，尽管这种规模的模型不会在那个规模下训练。实现这一点的各个部分并没有埋在一个配方里。SimpleFSDP、带 scan 的 Graph Trainer 和图分割器、主机卸载、Pallas 内核库和优化手册是构建模块，每一个都在一个标志之后，每一个都记录了它值多少数字。对于 TorchTitan 不提供的模型，Transformers 建模后端通过同一个训练器运行 500+ Hugging Face 模型，并已应用首批优化；对于想要更多的团队，接入技能将移植模型转变为工程师或代理可以遵循的可重复流程。

blocks.text: Model Definition Decoupled from Model Partitioning

inlines.text: Model Definition Decoupled from Model Partitioning

blocks.text: Model definitions in TorchTitan are written in pure, single-device PyTorch (nn.Module) with no CUDA-specific code. Collectives are inserted either by a composable framework layer (e.g. FSDP), by declarative sharding plans (e.g. tensor-parallelism), or as backend-specific plugins (e.g. MoE layers). TorchTPU supports C10D collective APIs and the PyTorch DeviceMesh abstraction. Together, this allows the TPU path to choose which parallelisms to apply for a model, and which implementations to use.

blocks.text: Pluggable Architecture

inlines.text: Pluggable Architecture

blocks.text: TorchTitan builds a model from a configuration tree, and that tree can be rewritten before the model is constructed. This offers a clean way to replace individual blocks of a model with versions that run better on TPU, without touching the model definition or the shared trainer loop.

blocks.text: We use this actively. The TPU recipes replace standard attention with Splash Attention, a Pallas kernel that handles causal, sliding-window and packed-document masks without materializing the attention matrix; replace the final projection and cross-entropy loss with a fused Pallas kernel that never writes the full logits tensor to HBM; and replace MoE expert matmuls with grouped Pallas kernels. blocks.text: Compile-Friendly FSDP Implementation

inlines.text: Compile-Friendly FSDP Implementation

blocks.text: FSDP2 is built around the GPU execution model. Its all-gathers and reduce-scatters are issued from module hooks as explicit collective calls, and overlap with compute comes from running them on dedicated CUDA streams synchronized with events. None of that is visible to a compiler: the collectives sit outside the traced region, so on TPU a torch.compile region breaks at every FSDP hook and a whole-step graph cannot be captured at all. TorchTPU provides no-op stream and event objects only so that FSDP2 runs; XLA has no use for them, since it schedules work from data dependencies.

blocks.text: SimpleFSDP takes the compiler's view instead. Parameter sharding is a DTensor parametrization: reading a module's weight performs a redistribute from sharded to replicated, which is the all-gather, and its autograd backward is the reduce-scatter. There are no hooks and no explicit collective calls, so both collectives are ordinary nodes in the traced graph, whether that graph is a per-block torch.compile region or the Graph Trainer's single make_fx step. The XLA compiler schedules the all-gathers ahead of the matmuls that need them and overlaps the reduce-scatters with the backward compute, inside one program. Mixed precision is part of the same mechanism, a policy that sets the gather dtype (bf16 parameters) and the reduce dtype (fp32 or bf16 gradients) on that redistribute. Hybrid sharding for multislice is the same code on a 2-D mesh: shard within a slice over ICI, replicate across slices over DCN.

blocks.text: 1. Establish a Baseline

inlines.text: 1. Establish a Baseline
Choose how the step executes: eager, compile, or Graph Trainer.

Eager mode runs PyTorch models on TPU with virtually no changes, which makes it the right place to bring a model up and debug it. It is not a performance configuration: every op is its own program and the TPU idles between launches. TorchTPU's
deferred-and-fused eager mode

(--tpu_config.eager_mode=DEFER_AND_FUSE) recovers some of that with no code change by letting XLA fuse across op boundaries, and the recipes keep it on to cover whatever sits outside compiled regions. Enabling
per-block torch.compile

(--compile.enable) is what turns a debug configuration into a performant one: each transformer block becomes a single XLA program, so its ops are fused, launched once instead of one at a time, and scheduled together with the block's collectives. The block has to trace, which rules out data-dependent Python inside it, and that is all the model gives up.
Graph Trainer goes further

(--tpu_config.use_graph_trainer) and lets the whole training step, forward, loss, backward and optimizer update, be captured as one program. The whole step has to trace, and what you get back is a step with no eager glue at all, plus the large-model techniques in step 5.
Shard with SimpleFSDP and a mixed-precision policy.
SimpleFSDP expresses

sharding as collectives inside the traced graph (--parallelism.use_simple_fsdp), so the compiler can schedule all-gathers and reduce-scatters against the matrix multiplies around them. FSDP2 itself is optimized for eager performance, but that also makes it difficult to trace into a graph. Pair it with bf16 parameters and fp32 gradient reduction: compute runs in bf16 while master weights and reductions stay in fp32, which is the setting every TPU recipe uses.
For large models (~100B+ parameters), enable scan or split the graph, and offload activations.
One unrolled step graph stops compiling as depth grows, and it keeps every layer's saved input live until the backward pass.
Scan over layers

(--tpu_config.use_scan_layers) runs the decoder as a single loop body, so compile time and memory stop growing with depth, and offloads the one stacked activation to host memory; this is the path Qwen3 235B and Llama 3 405B take.
The graph splitter

(--tpu_config.use_graph_split) keeps the layers unrolled but compiles forward and backward, and optionally each layer group, as separate programs with activations offloaded in between. Both build on Graph Trainer.

blocks.text: 2. Tune Compute and Kernals

inlines.text: 2. Tune Compute and Kernals
Turn on the Pallas kernels.
Splash attention

(--splash_attention_kernel.use_splash_attention_kernel) never materializes the attention matrix and handles causal, sliding-window and packed-document masks; it matters most at long sequence lengths. The
fused linear cross-entropy loss

(PallasCrossEntropyLoss in the recipe) computes the LM-head matmul, softmax and loss one vocabulary tile at a time, so the full logits tensor is never written to HBM. Its main value is memory, which the next step turns into throughput. For MoE models, the grouped expert matmul and the paired gate/up kernel (use_pallas_paired_grouped_mm) replace a loop over experts with one kernel per layer. Each of these is a switch in the recipe, and each is tested against the plain PyTorch path it replaces.
Tune the kernel tile sizes.

Splash attention, the fused loss and the MoE kernels each expose their block sizes (sa_block_* and friends), and the defaults are a starting point rather than an optimum. Tune them for the model shape and the TPU generation, within the scoped VMEM budget (xla_tpu_scoped_vmem_limit_kib), and expect values tuned on Trillium not to carry over to Ironwood. The recipes carry the tuned values for each model and topology.

blocks.text: 3. Optimize Memory and Batch Size

inlines.text: 3. Optimize Memory and Batch Size
Raise the batch.

At small scale the per-chip batch is the single largest lever, because it raises the work done per launched program. Push it until the model is HBM-bound; the fused loss and the attention kernel are what free the memory to do so. On a large slice, remember that the global batch is the per-chip batch times the chip count, so size it to what the model can use, not to what the chips can hold

blocks.text: 4. Tune Compiler, Communication and Profile

inlines.text: 4. Tune Compiler, Communication and Profile
Tune the
XLA and libtpu flags

Each recipe carries its flag bundle, such as the SparseCore latency-hiding scheduler and hierarchical reduce-scatter, with a comment explaining every flag, and --libtpu-init-flags lets you set flags from the command line. Flags never change what the model computes, but they can change how: a pure scheduling flag leaves the loss bit-identical, while a flag that alters fusion or the order of a reduction, hierarchical reduce-scatter being one, shifts rounding. So check the step-1 loss and gradient norm after every sweep. Bit-identical means the flag is free. A small difference means a rounding-order change, which is only safe once a loss-curve comparison against the baseline recipe says so.
Profile, find the bottleneck, and go back to the lever that addresses it.
Capture an xprof trace
over a few steady-state steps (--profiler.enable_profiling); the
TorchTPU profiling guide
covers capture on TorchTPU and the
xprof documentation
covers the tools. The trace answers one question: where does the step time go? Two references take it from there: the
Cloud TPU performance guide
explains the XLA-level levers (padding, tensor dimensions, batch size, fusion) and when each applies, and the scaling book's chapter
How to Profile TPU Programs
shows how to read a TPU trace op by op.

inlines.text: FLUX.1

blocks.text: FLUX.1 is a 12-billion-parameter diffusion transformer, which makes it a useful check that the playbook above is not specific to LLMs. We trained it at 1024x1024 resolution on a TPU v6e-8 with FSDP in bf16 and a batch of three samples. Out of the box, in eager mode with FSDP2 and full activation checkpointing, a step took 11.49 seconds. Applying the playbook in order brought that down one stage at a time. Deferred-and-fused eager execution cut the number of HLO module invocations by 28% and the step to 9.95 s (15.5% improvement). Replacing FSDP2 with SimpleFSDP reduced the step to 6.52 s (52.6% improvement): the trace was dominated by FSDP2 copying parameter shards into a flat staging buffer before each all-gather and back out into per-parameter tensors afterwards; SimpleFSDP all-gathers each parameter directly, so the staging buffer and both copies are gone (see the SimpleFSDP section above). The splash attention kernel, with sequence packing and segment ids so that no MXU cycles go to padding, took the step to 5.55 s (17.5% improvement), and per-block torch.compile, which hands XLA large sub-graphs instead of fine-grained modules and moves control flow out of the Python interpreter, took it to 3.02 s (83.8% improvement).

blocks.text: MuseGlimmer

inlines.text: MuseGlimmer

blocks.text: Muse Glimmer 30B is a modern dense decoder: 52 layers, grouped-query attention with 32 query and 2 key-value heads, a 202k-token vocabulary with a soft-capped output head, and a layer pattern that mixes sliding-window and global attention, with RoPE skipped on every fourth layer. It is the case that shows how much works out of the box. The model definition, the parallelization and the training loop ran on TPU unchanged; the port came down to two model-specific pieces. Upstream implements the sliding-window pattern with FlexAttention, which has no TPU backend, so the first step was a windowed SDPA inner attention that reproduces the window exactly and gives a correctness baseline, checked against upstream on CPU. The second piece was the fused cross-entropy kernel, which we extended to apply the soft-cap to each vocabulary tile as it computes the loss, so the 202k-wide logits never have to be materialized; without that the LM head alone dominated memory. Everything else, including the Graph Trainer wrapper, was the standard onboarding ladder, with each feature behind a flag and its own test. The resulting recipe trains the 30B on 64 v7x chips (a 4x4x4 slice) at sequence length 16,384 with one sequence per device, Graph Trainer plus SimpleFSDP and fp32 gradient reductions, and reaches 5,848 tokens per second per chip at ~44% MFU.

blocks.text: Qwen3 235B

inlines.text: Qwen3 235B

blocks.text: Qwen3-235B-A22B is the largest MOE model in this set: 94 layers, 128 experts with 8 active per token, 235 billion parameters of which 22 billion are active per token. It is the case that exercises the large-model half of the playbook. At this depth compiling the whole unrolled step as one program is not an option: XLA plans every buffer of a program at compile time, and a 94-layer graph laid out flat asks for more HBM than the chip has before a step can run, while its compile time grows with every layer. Getting it to work at all meant enabling one of the two Graph Trainer paths for large models. Scan over layers is the XLA-native answer, the same construct JAX and MaxText rely on: the 94 identical layers become one compiled loop body, so compile time and program size stop growing with depth. The graph splitter is the more flexible alternative: it keeps the layers unrolled but cuts the captured step into per-layer executables, which works no matter what kind of layers you have (and does not require layers to be the same). We run both for this model and they land within a few percent of each other. Either way the activations do not fit in HBM at sequence length 4096 with 16 sequences per device, so both paths offload layer activations to host memory and prefetch them back for the backward pass.

blocks.text: From there the playbook applied, one change at a time, each measured on the same 64-chip slice. We raised the scoped VMEM budget so the compiler could keep more kernel intermediates on chip, which also removed an exposed update at the tail of the optimizer step. We enabled a set of libtpu scheduling flags that let XLA's latency-hiding scheduler overlap the FSDP all-gathers and reduce-scatters with the surrounding compute and offload the reduce-scatters to the SparseCores, so most of the collective time is hidden behind compute, leaving only a small exposed reduce-scatter tail in the backward pass. We switched attention to the tokamax splash kernel, and replaced the expert matmuls with specialized paired grouped-matmul kernels backed by a K-tiled weight-gradient kernel, with hierarchical reduce-scatter and the SparseCore latency-hiding scheduler to hide the expert-gradient collectives. A fused route-score backward removed a large fp32 copy from the MoE backward pass. The last round of fixes came from profiling at 1,024 chips: keeping the blocked activation layout under scan offload, raising the backward layer-scheduler threshold so the expert reduce-scatters overlap with compute again, and pipelining small reduce-scatters across the scan loop's back-edge. The recipe runs at ~32% MFU on 256 v7x chips with fp32 gradient reductions kept throughout.

blocks.text: We also used this model to test how far TorchTPU scales, from 64 chips up to 8,192-chip v7x pod scale, in both single-slice and multi-slice configurations. A TPU slice is a set of chips connected directly over the inter-chip interconnect (ICI); multislice lets one training job span several slices connected over the data-center network (DCN), which is how a job grows past the largest single slice. Within a slice we run FSDP over ICI, sharding parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the slice's chips; across slices the model is replicated and the gradients are all-reduced over DCN once per step, so the only traffic on the slower network is a single gradient reduction, which overlaps with the backward pass. That is hybrid sharded data parallelism (HSDP), and it is what the 2,048- to 8,192-chip runs use, with 1,024-chip slices as the sharding group. The framework behaved as expected throughout: per-chip throughput dropped by 8% going from 64 to 8,192 chips (4,568 to 4,208 tokens per second per chip), near-linear scaling across 128x more chips. One caveat: for a model of this size, data parallelism beyond about 1K chips is a scaling experiment rather than a training recipe. This is a weak-scaling run: the batch per device stays fixed as chips are added, so the global batch grows with the chip count and at 8k chips is larger than one would use to train this model. What the run shows is that the framework, the compiler and the collectives hold up at that scale, not that this is the configuration to train with.

data-center network (DCN)

, which is how a job grows past the largest single slice. Within a slice we run FSDP over ICI, sharding parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the slice's chips; across slices the model is replicated and the gradients are all-reduced over DCN once per step, so the only traffic on the slower network is a single gradient reduction, which overlaps with the backward pass. That is
hybrid sharded data parallelism (HSDP)

, and it is what the 2,048- to 8,192-chip runs use, with 1,024-chip slices as the sharding group. The framework behaved as expected throughout: per-chip throughput dropped by 8% going from 64 to 8,192 chips (4,568 to 4,208 tokens per second per chip), near-linear scaling across 128x more chips. One caveat: for a model of this size, data parallelism beyond about 1K chips is a scaling experiment rather than a training recipe. This is a weak-scaling run: the batch per device stays fixed as chips are added, so the global batch grows with the chip count and at 8k chips is larger than one would use to train this model. What the run shows is that the framework, the compiler and the collectives hold up at that scale, not that this is the configuration to train with.

blocks.text: HuggingFace Transformers modeling backend for TorchTitan TPU

inlines.text: HuggingFace Transformers modeling backend for TorchTitan TPU

blocks.text: The three case studies above are deep dives: one model at a time, with a parity test and a profile behind every change. A team arriving on TPU usually has a different problem. They have a model they already train, often a Hugging Face one, and quite likely it won’t be the model that TorchTitan ships for TPU. They may well want every last percent out of it eventually, but first they need an easy way to get it running at all. That is the problem the Transformers modeling backend solves: it builds the model from the Transformers library by its Hub id and runs it through TorchTitan's trainer and parallelism instead of its own. On TPU the backend has a TorchTPU lane with a single configuration that applies the first rungs of the playbook optimizations to any supported checkpoint, with no change to the model code: SimpleFSDP in place of FSDP2, per-block torch.compile, the splash attention kernel registered as an attention implementation with the transformers attention interface so the model's own attention calls land on it, the fused Pallas cross entropy fed the final hidden states and the head weight instead of materialized logits, and, for mixture-of-experts checkpoints, the TPU grouped-matmul experts substituted for the portable implementation. Most of the dense architectures the backend supports train this way unmodified; mixture-of-experts checkpoints run through the same path but without expert parallelism yet. None of this reaches the hand-tuned numbers above, but it is a working, reasonably efficient first run for a model that has no TPU recipe yet, and a way to find out whether it deserves one.

inlines.text: Agent-assisted Model Onboarding to TorchTitan TPU

blocks.text: Sooner or later a model deserves more than a generic path: it is the one you will train for months, it has an architecture the backend cannot express, or the out-of-the-box number is not the one you need. Porting a model to a new accelerator used to be a specialist project measured in weeks, with the hard-won lessons living in one engineer's head. On TorchTitan TPU it is a repeatable procedure. The repository ships a model-onboarding skill for coding agents that captures how the case studies above were done and walks an engineer, or the agent itself, through the same ladder, with the tests, the acceptance bars and the traps built in.

blocks.text: Roadmap

inlines.text: Roadmap

blocks.text: The roadmap runs along five lines: production readiness, precision, hardware, parallelism and models. On production readiness, the recipes gain the operational tooling that long runs on Google Cloud expect: integration with the ML Goodput Measurement library, so a run reports how much of its chip time turns into preserved training progress and where the rest goes, and with Multi-Tier Checkpointing on GKE, which keeps checkpoints in local memory and in-cluster replicas with Cloud Storage as the durable tier, so large jobs save often and resume quickly. On precision, the float8 recipe that today ships for Llama 3 70B, built on torchao's Float8Linear and v7x's native fp8 matmuls, extends to the rest of the model set. On hardware, Google has announced its eighth-generation TPUs, TPU 8t for pre-training and TPU 8i for inference and reinforcement learning, and TorchTitan will support them as they become available on Google Cloud, with the same recipes carried forward. On parallelism, expert parallelism for the MoE kernels is the open item named earlier, and long-context training is next after it, now that million-token context windows are the norm for frontier models. On models, the targets are the next size up from Qwen3-235B: Qwen3.8-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture of experts, and Kimi K3, 2.8 trillion parameters with Kimi Delta Attention in place of standard attention on most layers, which will exercise the kernel plug-in path as much as the scaling one.

blocks.text: Summary

inlines.text: Summary

blocks.text: TorchTitan on TPU is no longer an experiment. The same codebase and plain-PyTorch model definitions train Llama 3 405B at about 57% MFU on up to 1,024 chips, and run Qwen3 235B, a mixture-of-experts model, on up to 1,024 chips in a single slice. In a weak-scaling test with a fixed per-chip batch, Qwen3 235B kept 92% of its per-chip throughput from 64 to 8,192 chips. That shows the framework, compiler and collectives hold up at pod scale, even though a model of this size would not be trained at that scale. The pieces that make this possible are not buried in one recipe. SimpleFSDP, the Graph Trainer with scan and the graph splitter, host offload, the Pallas kernel library and the optimization playbook are building blocks, each behind a flag and each documented with the number it is worth. For models that TorchTitan does not ship, the Transformers modeling backend runs 500+ Hugging Face models through the same trainer with the first optimizations already applied, and for teams that want more than that, the onboarding skill turns porting a model into a repeatable procedure that an engineer or an agent can follow.

blocks.text: That leaves two ways to use it. The first is to adopt TorchTitan as the training framework: pick a recipe, launch it on a slice, and build on a configuration whose performance is already known. The second is to keep the training code you have and take what you need: the kernels are standard PyTorch custom ops, SimpleFSDP and the Graph Trainer are modules you can import, the compiler flags and the playbook apply to any TorchTPU workload, and every recipe spells out what it enables and why. Either way, the fastest way to find out what this does for your model is to run it.
